title: What are you doing tomorrow?
goal: Make plans and talk about the weather, using the three ways Romanian expresses the future — and knowing which one people actually use in conversation.
bekal: state plans with *o să* + subjunctive: *o să merg, o să meargă, o să fie*
recognize the formal future *voi, vei, va, vom, veți, vor* + infinitive in the news and weather forecasts
talk about the weather, seasons, and months, including *mi-e cald* and *mi-e frig*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Planuri de weekend

notes: **O să merg.** This is the future Romanians use when they chat: the little word *o*, which **never changes**, then *să* and the subjunctive from unit 11 — much like English "going to". Since the subjunctive only differs in the third person, that's practically the only place to watch: *o să **fie** înnorat* (not *este*), *o să **bată** vântul* (not *bate*). *O să plouă* happens to be safe, because the subjunctive *plouă* is the same as the present.

**Plecăm dimineața cu trenul — present tense for the future.** When the time is clear from a time word or context, the present is enough, just as in English "we're leaving tomorrow". The question *Ce faci mâine?* itself is in the present. It's the easiest way, and not a lazy one at all.

**Voi veni la ora șase.** The future with *voi* is the formal, written form. In conversation it sounds solemn, like English "I shall" — which is why Ioana uses it jokingly to make a promise. You'll **read** it more often than say it: in the news, office emails, and weather forecasts (*Mâine va ploua*).

**Dacă e frumos, o să ieșim.** After *dacă* (if) the present is enough; the future goes in the other half of the sentence, as in English. *A ieși* (go out) is a little irregular: *ies, ieși, iese, ieșim, ieșiți, ies*, third-person subjunctive *să iasă*.

**E cald, e urât, e soare — sentences with no subject.** For weather Romanian needs no "it": just *e* (short for *este*) + a description. *Urât* literally means "ugly", *frumos* "beautiful": *e urât afară* = the weather outside is bad. And in Romania the wind doesn't "blow", it "beats": *bate vântul*.

grammars.title: The everyday future — *o să* + subjunctive
body: English marks the future with a helper that never changes ("will", "going to"). *O să* works almost the same way: *o* stays put, and only the verb after *să* conjugates — in forms you've known since unit 11.
This table deliberately includes *a fi*, the only verb whose subjunctive differs in **every** person.
after: **Negative:** *nu* before *o*, merging in speech: *Nu o să vin* = *N-o să vin*. *Mâine n-o să plouă.*

**The little pronouns go between *să* and the verb**, just as in units 11 and 12: *o să **mă** întorc târziu*, *o să **te** aștept la gară*, *o să **ne** întâlnim la șase*. After *să*, *îl* usually shortens to *-l* and *o* merges: *o să-l văd*, *o s-o văd*.
**The third-person subjunctives you'll need most here:** *vine → o să vină*, *face → o să facă*, *stă → o să stea*, *are → o să aibă*, *ia → o să ia*, *ninge → o să ningă*, *rămâne → o să rămână*.
On the street you'll also hear its twin, *am să merg, ai să mergi, are să meargă…* Same meaning. Just recognize it; for speaking, *o să* is more than enough.

grammars.title: The formal future — *voi, vei, va, vom, veți, vor* + infinitive
body: This is the "grammar book" future: a conjugated helper followed by the infinitive **without *a***. It lives in writing, speeches, announcements, and weather forecasts.
after: **Don't mix it up with *a vrea*.** *Vor* means both "they want" and the future helper; the difference is *să*: *vor **să** vină* (they want to come) versus *vor veni* (they will come). And *voi* is also the pronoun "you (plural)", so *voi veți veni* is perfectly fine: "you will come".

**The negative and little pronouns stand before the helper**, with no merging: *nu voi veni*, *mă voi întoarce în septembrie*, *îl voi vedea mâine*. Even *o* behaves and goes in front here: *o voi vedea*.

**After *dacă*:** in conversation use the present — *Dacă plouă, stăm acasă* or *…o să stăm acasă*. In formal writing you'll also see *dacă va ploua*; both are correct. What never comes right after *dacă* is *să*.
In short, for A1 learners: **say** the present or *o să*, **recognize** *voi veni* when reading. Nobody will think you impolite for using *o să* with Mrs. Popescu.

Say it
English
rows: The weather's nice. · The weather's bad.

blocks.text: All three times are now in your hands: *Ieri a plouat. Azi plouă. Mâine o să plouă.* Likewise *a nins · ninge · o să ningă* and *a fost cald · e cald · o să fie cald*. The nouns: *ploaie* (rain), *zăpadă* or *ninsoare* (snow), *vânt* (wind), *nor* (cloud), *furtună* (storm). Temperatures are in Celsius.

**Never say *sunt cald* or *sunt frig*.** For how you feel, Romanian uses the dative from unit 10: *mi-e frig*, literally "to me it is cold". The cold happens to you; it isn't what you are — *sunt rece* would mean "I am a cold person". *E frig* = the air is cold; *Mi-e frig* = I'm cold. The negative is *Nu mi-e frig*. The same pattern comes back in unit 17 for hungry, thirsty, and sleepy.

blocks.title: Four real seasons
items: Romania has a continental climate: Bucharest summers often top 35 degrees Celsius (95°F), and winters can drop far below zero, snow included. Both take some preparing for.
Two words that often turn up in the news: *caniculă* (heat wave) and *viscol* (blizzard).

Official weather warnings are color-coded: *cod galben* (yellow), *cod portocaliu* (orange), and *cod roșu* (red). If your phone buzzes with a *cod roșu de furtună* message, postpone the trip to the park.

blocks.text: A season name with the article means "in that season", just like *dimineața* and *sâmbăta*: *Vara merg la mare, iarna merg la munte.* Month names are written in **lowercase** and are close cousins of the English ones. "In a month" = *în*: *în august, în decembrie*. Dates use *pe* + an ordinary number: *pe 15 august*, *pe 24 ianuarie*. Only the first is special: *pe **întâi** mai* (not *unu*).

blocks.title: March 1: *Mărțișor*
items: On *întâi martie* Romanians welcome spring with the *mărțișor*: a tiny trinket tied with a twisted **red-and-white** string. It's given mainly to women — mothers, coworkers, teachers — and pinned to the chest for the first days of March. The name itself means "little March".

Ioana is sure to get a few at the office, so have one ready and say: *O primăvară frumoasă!* ("Have a lovely spring!"). Since 2017 the tradition has been on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage.

The first nine days of March are called *Babele* ("the old women"). Pick a date from 1 to 9: according to old belief, the weather that day predicts your year — sunny means an easy year, rainy means a gloomy one.
